utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we commence with your testimony, which will be interrupted very soon because we will be having a break, I would like to provide you with some information concerning the procedure we will be following here. I would first like to apologise to you because your testimony should have commenced at 2.15, but as we had certain technical matters to deal with, your testimony can only be commenced now. But we believe that we will be able to examine you in the course of the afternoon. As I have already said, you are appearing here as a witness for the Defence. You will first of all have to answer questions put to you by Defence counsel. Both Defence teams may ask you questions if they wish to. At the end of this stage, the Prosecution, who are to your right, will commence with their cross-examination. The Judges sitting before you may ask you questions at any point in time, but as a rule the Judges prefer to wait for both parties to complete their examination before putting questions to witnesses. When Judges ask a witness questions, this is in order to help us in establishing the truth. There are also two other factors I would like to point out to you: You have taken the solemn declaration. You have said that you will speak the truth and this means you shouldn't give false testimony. As you know, false testimony constitutes an offence which is punishable. There's another thing I should point out to you: When a witness is asked to answer a question, if the witness believes that his answer might provide information that could incriminate him at a subsequent date, in such a case the witness can refuse to answer the question. But in such exceptional circumstances, the Trial Chamber may nevertheless compel the witness to answer the question but the witness is granted a form of immunity. I just wanted to point this out to you. So far this has never been an issue. In addition, try to answer the questions put to you as clearly and precisely as possible because the procedure that we follow here is adversarial but the procedure is oral, so what you say is important. Everything you say is transcribed. You will see your answers appearing on the screen before you. The transcript of what you say is in English. When you are being examined, you might be shown certain documents, documents, for example, of military nature. Feel free to answer the questions. Don't be concerned, everything will go well, everything has gone well so far. We'll now have a break, 20- or 25-minute break, not because we want to have a rest but it is necessary to have a break for technical reasons. If everything depended just on me, we would continue. So we will have a 20- or 25-minute break now and we will resume at about 5 to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will now resume and I will give the floor to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Kulenovic. In addition to the words you heard from the Presiding Judge, I am going to ask you to make a short pause after my question. In other words, wait for my question to be translated for the Trial Chamber and for everybody else in the courtroom. Did you understand that?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have told us that you were an officer of the former JNA. Please tell us, which schools did you finish, when and where?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was a JNA officer. I completed primary school, secondary aviation school, I completed a military academy in Belgrade. After that, I was given the rank of a second lieutenant in the JNA. After that I completed a number of courses. I continued my education while I worked in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Which branch of the army did you serve in?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: I completed education for the army officer, and I belonged to the sabotage and reconnaissance unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you serve while in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: When I completed my education I was sent to Slovenia, and this is where I served, namely in the towns of Celje, Novo Mesto, Ljubljana and Posnjna. These are little towns in the Republic of Slovenia where I served as a JNA officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kulenovic, did there come a time when you left the JNA; and if that is the case, why did you leave it?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I left the JNA on the 6th of April, 1992. I have to explain that I survived. I personally witnessed whatever was taking place when Yugoslavia started breaking up. I was in Slovenia when the war broke out in Slovenia and it was already there that I noticed - and not only me but also the majority of other officers - that this was not the same JNA for which I was educated and for which I had worked for 13 years. In the -- I arrived in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina amongst the last units that had left the territory of the Republic of Slovenia. I was sent to serve in Kraljevo, which is a town in Serbia. From there I was assigned to the command of the 7th army in Sarajevo. This was sometime in November 1991. I was placed at the disposal -- I don't know whether you are familiar with that term. I was placed at the disposal of the command of the troops in Sarajevo. I was assigned to the Lukavica barracks in Sarajevo. After some two or three months, I spent some time in Lukavica between November and March. I did not have any particular tasks during that time. After that, I was assigned to the Zenica barracks. And from Zenica, on the 4th of April, 1992, I left the JNA, I deflected, I ran away. I can go into more details if you wish me to.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. This will not be necessary. Once you left the JNA, did you join some armed forces? If that is the case, can you tell us which armed forces those were.

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: When I left the JNA from the barracks in Zenica on the 6th of April, I reported to the staff of Territorial Defence in Vitez, which is my native place. That's where I reported. I believe this was on the 8th of April, so two days after I ran. I have to say that I reported to the staff of the Territorial Defence, but I had to go into hiding for a few days because the then-commander of the Zenica barracks, Colonel Sipcic was looking after me. He was looking for me in the region of Travnik and Vitez. There were threats against my family. So these were all things that accompanied my running away from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of April the JNA and the Serbian forces had already attacked Bosnia and Herzegovina; this is not in dispute. When you reported to the staff of the Territorial Defence in Vitez, did you assume any duties? If that is the case, what duties did you assume?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: When I reported to the Territorial Defence Staff in Vitez, as far as I could understand the Territorial Defence had not yet been organised in the way it should have been organised. People reported to the staff and people were placed at the disposal of the republican bodies and they were waiting for their assignment. That means that I was not deployed for some five or six days. Then the staff commander called me and asked me to establish a manoeuvre detachment of the Vitez defence staff, consisting of some 200 to 250 people who would be engaged in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I had some organisational problems while I was establishing this unit. I have to emphasise here that we did not have any weapons. What we had were a few rifles, few hunting rifles, a few revolvers, few pistols, and that was all that we had by way of weapons in our unit. In terms of organisation, I tried to establish this unit as well as I could.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kulenovic, did you remain in Vitez or did you soon after that change the place of residence, did you change your assignment in the Territorial Defence as well?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: When this manoeuvre detachment was established in Vitez, which happened on the 21st or 22nd of April, 1992, and since there had already been combat activities taking place, the BiH army and its bodies had already started fighting the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor, and since there had already been operations near Vitez in Travnik, in Turbe, on the pass towards Novi Travnik, towards the end of April and the beginning of May - I can't remember the date - I was still engaged together with one part of my unit in the Turbe front line. We -- our shift lasted for five to seven days, or eight days. This is where I was engaged for the first time. After that, I was engaged together with my manoeuvre detachment in the Visoko front line between the 20th of May, 1992, and the end of August. My detachment was there in shifts. This is in the region of the town of Visoko, or to be more specific, in Crkcici [phoen], which is a settlement there, and this is where I stayed until the end of August. Towards the end of August or the beginning of September at my own request or, in other words, at the request of the commander of the defence staff of Travnik and pursuant to the approval of the command of the regional staff of Zenica, I was transferred to the municipal staff of Travnik and I was appointed at the assistant commander for education and operations. In other words, I prepared and monitored combat activities that took place in that territory and the area of responsibility of the municipal defence staff of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Only briefly can you tell us whether you stayed in the municipal staff for a while and did you assume any other duties besides the one that you have mentioned?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: You mean in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I mean in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: In Travnik, when I arrived in the Travnik staff at the beginning of September, I stayed in that position sometime until mid-November, until the 18th of November when the municipality of Jajce fell together with some parts of municipality of Travnik, namely the Karaula settlement. Because some problems appeared in the municipal staff, the then-commander of staff was ill and had to be taken to hospital, on the 18th of November, Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond pursuant to an order, I was appointed a commander of the defence staff of Travnik. Towards the end of November I became the commander of the defence staff of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Kulenovic, since you were an officer in the JNA, all of a sudden you found yourself in the Territorial Defence. Did you have any information at the time as to what the Territorial Defence was? And how did you accept your new role in the Territorial Defence as staff?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: During my military education and during my active service in the former JNA, I had a lot of information and I gained quite a lot of knowledge on the role, tasks, and position of the Territorial Defence within the former Yugoslavia. When I arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina and after all of these developments, the role and the function of the Territorial Defence changed. The Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina assumed some other characteristics. I know that in the former system the commander of the municipal staff was a member of the War Presidency. In the new organisational system of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the staff commander did -- was not a member of the War Presidency of the municipality. However, he could exert influence and he could work towards organising the Defence when it came to working with the bodies of civilian power and the War Presidency. So this is just a rough outline.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since in my further examination I will be using certain documents, I would kindly ask the usher to distribute the documents. We have a set of documents that will be shown to this witness and we have copies for everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to my previous question you said that some changes did take place when we're talking about the structure of the Territorial Defence and the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina with regard to the previous system of general people's defence. In 1992 and the best part of 1993 you spent in the municipal staff of the Territorial Defence. Can you tell me whether the civilian bodies of power that had been in the position to organise defence, did they come to terms with the changes that you have just talked about? If you have any information about that, can you please share that information with us briefly.

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were interference. There was certain overlapping of duties, and civilian bodies of power interfered with the work of the military bodies. In my view, civilian bodies didn't want to relegate some of their authorities and privileges that they enjoyed when it came to controlling the army and those civilian bodies that were involved in working with the army. There are a number of examples to illustrate that, however, it suffices for me to say that the civilian bodies, for example in Travnik, on one occasion issued an order to me, or attempted to issue orders to me to do this or that or the other with regard to certain military aspects of the front line. They ordered me to engage units or equipment, or they would say that because of the safety of the citizens, certain pieces of equipment had to be relocated, or they would tell me that the route for those artillery pieces when they went to the front line could not be by certain villages but that a different route had to be taken. This was an interference and a direct interference with the military matters. And they also tried to influence the personnel. For example, they -- if there was an officer who was a reserve officer or a former active officer of the JNA, they would tell me this person had to be placed here or there. So as I'm saying there was interference and overlapping in terms of equipment, in terms of deploying staff, and in professional military terms, this is not correct. I fought that. Sometimes I had to resort to somewhat rougher means. Let me just say that they didn't want to give up some of their privileges and rights.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at document number 9 referring to the BiH army. The number of this document is 0591 -- 0951. As you can see, this is a decision of the War Presidency of the Travnik municipality, and it was issued in April 1993. Can you please look at the decision and tell me, given what you have just testified about, which is the interference of the civilian bodies when it came to military matters, how do you see this decision? Does this decision reflect the situation that you have just testified about?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: I'm familiar with this document. I was provided with it at some point in time when I needed it. And even then I said that they couldn't issue orders to me. I said I have my superiors and my subordinates, I had superiors who would issue orders to me. But if I may provide you with an explanation. With regard to the orders that I received earlier on and have to do with this order from the 3rd Corps command to form certain units, to change certain structures, et cetera, et cetera, I was already working on the formation of these so-called area units. And at the time they were in preparatory stage, we were preparing to form them. So this specific order issued by the War Presidency has a certain weight in that this is what should have been organised, but things weren't done in accordance with the competencies of various people and various bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kulenovic, the War Presidency or the municipality, what sort of responsibilities did they have according to the law with regard to army units? What was their duty with regard to the army? What were they to provide the army with in order to enable the army to perform its function?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: In accordance with the new law that was adopted for the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the municipality was primarily responsible for providing logistical support for operative units. They had to provide them with technical equipment and materiel, they had to provide them with ammunition, they had to provide them with transport to certain points. So they had to provide them with food, clothes, et cetera, et cetera. This was a logistical role that had to be played. These are the main things that the municipality had to provide the BH army with at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who carried out the mobilisation of men and equipment for the army?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: I should have mentioned mobilisation. Men and equipment was mobilised at the request of the municipal staff by the municipal defence organ. It was the municipality's task to mobilise men and equipment and to place them at the disposal of operative units. In this specific case, at the disposal of the Territorial Defence municipal staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at document number 14. The number of the document is 1169. Tell me, is this a document that refers to the responsibilities and authorities that the War Presidency of the civilian body had in relation to the army? And you have just spoken about this in your previous answer.

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And this document states quite specifically what the municipal staff or the Secretariat for National Defence should do. It should say finding heavy machines, but we had machines that were in certain construction companies; shovels, excavators, bulldozers, et cetera, everything that was needed to arrange defence lines facing the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor. We would request such equipment from the municipal organ, and it was their duty to obtain such equipment. I am familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At some point towards the end of 1992, were there any changes in the organisation of the army, and what position did you hold at the time?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: At the end of 1992, I don't know the exact date because there were communication problems, it was difficult to deliver mail, et cetera, but certain organisational changes, significant organisational changes, were made. The Territorial Defence municipal staffs, which were not sufficiently linked up in an overall system of defence - this is my opinion - the supreme command and my immediate command, the 3rd Corps command, ordered that operative units should be formed. I don't know what the exact name was, but I know that my municipal Territorial Defence staff in Travnik had to form two operation units, a motorised brigade and a mountain brigade. On the basis of that order, we formed those two brigades, the 312th Motorised Brigade with the zone of responsibility in Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Travnik and in the Turbe area, and it's in that part of the territory that equipment and men were mobilised; and that was the 306th Mountain Brigade that was formed, which was present in the Bila area. The Vlasic plateau, Mehurici, Han Bila, and the other mountainous part, that's where it was located. And out of the remains of the municipal staff -- well, the municipal Territorial Defence staff continued to function in a reduced capacity.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kulenovic, you said that the civilian bodies tried to influence the municipal staff. Tell me whether at that time influence was exerted on the army's operative units, and in which units was this influence most pronounced if there was -- such influence was exerted?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: I'll have to repeat something I've already said. The municipal bodies tried to have as much influence as possible on the structure and the functioning of the army. When the order was received to form operative units, we decided who the commanders would be, who the commanders of the operative units would be, this was decided at certain meetings, and in cooperation with civilian bodies we would appoint certain people to keep posts in brigades, and in this way we tried to separate the municipal bodies. And I think we managed to separate the municipal civilian bodies from the operative units. Given the conditions that prevailed, the influence of the civilian bodies was not as great on the operative units. In a certain sense, they were placed within a system of subordination, but nevertheless there was still considerable influence on the municipal staff. They would still meddle in military matters in the Territorial Defence staff. This is what the municipal bodies of the civilian authorities would do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We have heard a number of testimonies on a great number of refugees arriving in Travnik. Can you tell us how those people organised themselves and whether there was influence in the brigades which was formed by displaced persons to a large extent, and I'm referring to the Travnik area in particular.

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to provide you with a more detailed explanation. When I was assigned as the commander of the Travnik municipal staff at the end of November, I think that over 30.000 displaced persons passed through the territory of the municipality of Travnik. I would like to point out that receiving these refugees and accommodating them was a problem. It was also a problem to send them on. And the municipal staff and operative brigades were burdened by this problem. The municipal bodies had quite a lot of influence on the reception of refugees, and to a certain extent this was their duty, but the municipal defence staff in Travnik also had such responsibilities. The influence they had displaced persons -- first of all I should point out they were accommodated in the gymnasia, in private houses as well, and we had a lot of problems. The municipal bodies tried to have an influence on the fate of these displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kulenovic, tell me, in addition to the normal civilian bodies of power in Travnik, did some other bodies start appearing, bodies from areas from which people had been displaced, and what was their attitude towards these refugees, towards these displaced persons?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the territory of Travnik and in the wider area, the displaced or the expelled persons were mostly from Banja Luka, Prijedor, and some smaller towns, Kotor Varos, et cetera, and the political bodies from those areas were temporarily stopped in Travnik. And I know that the Banja Luka region and the Prijedor region were particularly active in the sense of politically organising displaced persons. They wanted to take charge of these expelled persons, and as the situation developed they even wanted to form their own brigades, with headquarters in Travnik or somewhere else in the free territory. And this caused us significant problems in terms of organisation and materiel and equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have just said that you had problems. All these attempts to form various military organisations, armies, under the influence of civilian authorities, did this make it more difficult for you to establish regular units in the area of Travnik or did this take place in spite of your engagements?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to provide you with a lengthy explanation. We were working on the formation of operative units, on structuring them, on finding the men, training the men. We were doing everything necessary to form operative units and put into function the staff. At the same time, numerous refugees had arrived from occupied areas; Banja Luka, Prijedor, et cetera. And while forming the units, we also had to have parts of units which would receive refugees or displaced and expelled persons. These people would arrive at the demarcation line separating us from the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor. So in addition to forming these units, we had care for the expelled persons. So I as the commander of the municipal staff who was responsible for forming units was never able to establish a brigade. I had to restructure these organisations, other commanders had to do this, too, so the largest unit we were able to establish at the time and call them a company or a battalion of such-and-such brigade and assign them certain responsibilities, the largest unit we could establish was a company consisting of 150 men. And this was just before the parts of these units would go to the defence lines. So this is how we established the units. And while conducting this defensive war, we formed those units. A few times when the unit was returning from the lines, I would sometimes return displaced persons from the lines, not just the troops. So the troops and the civilians were mixed up. Naturally, there were a lot of rumours that were then spread and there was propaganda, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kulenovic, please have a look at document number 2 in the first series of documents. The number of the document is 472. It's a document from the War Presidency of Banja Luka municipality; it was drafted in Zagreb. Tell me whether such a request made -- was this one of the requests that you would find, was this one where the political bodies tried to influence the army structure?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: This is the first time I've seen this document. The Presidency of the municipality of Banja Luka, with its headquarters in Zagreb, requested that a Banja Luka brigade be formed. Naturally, I expected to receive certain orders from my immediate superior command. This is the first time I see this document, but I know there were rumours and I know that in contact with the civilian authorities in Banja Luka and in Prijedor, I know that they said that they would like to form their own brigades, that they would like to have their own units, but this is the first time I've seen this document. In any event, this one of the documents that indicates that displaced persons wanted to fight, they wanted to have their own brigades, and if they weren't placed within the system of control and command, naturally such orders would have a negative influence on the events unfolding in the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at document number 3 in the same series. The number of the document is 473. It's a decision of the staff of the supreme command, according to which the 1st Banja Luka Brigade is to be formed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Again, I must say that this is the first time I've seen this document. And I as a professional member of the military would have to respect such a document, naturally. This document contains all elements that an official order should contain. There is the appropriate heading and mention is made of an authorised person, Sefer Halilovic, in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a commander of the municipal staff, during that year did you come across other orders on forming numerous refugee brigades in the territory of Travnik municipality; and when you came across such orders, did you know what sort of information the staff of the supreme command in Sarajevo actually had about the events in the field?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: I can understand your question, but I would answer it as follows: In Travnik the 312th and 306th Brigade were formed, the 17th Krajina Brigade was also formed on the basis of orders issued by my superiors, and I saw that there were orders on the formation of the 27th Brigade, too. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond This occurred subsequently. I also saw orders on the formation of the 37th Mountain Brigade. As far as the orders are concerned relating to the formation of brigades in Travnik and the wider area, I'm not familiar with all the orders, I don't know what the supreme command staff in Sarajevo ordered. I wasn't able to know about this and I didn't know about this, but I know what my immediate superior, the 3rd Corps command, ordered. And I carried out the orders issued by the 3rd Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at document 0774. It's document number 7. You mentioned the 27th Motorised Brigade, which was also to be formed of refugees. Tell me, how long did this process last from the time when the first initiatives were taken up until the formation of this brigade?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: The process to establish a brigade should be explained in somewhat greater detail. When I served in the JNA for 13 years, I experienced two or three organisational changes. In the JNA we had everything; we had facilities, we had equipment, everything that was necessary for an organised military. And this process took months. As far as I could know as a company commander and then captain, when a unit is established in the conditions of war, when nobody knew who was in charge or what was going on, the process to form a brigade was a tall order. It was an impossible situation. However, we managed to establish a brigade despite the problems. As I can see here, the order was issued at the beginning of March and the units became operational towards the end of 1993, in September or maybe October, I don't know exactly. I only know that one part of the command became operational in May and its units became operational subsequently. I have to say that the 27th Brigade should have been established from the refugees from Kotor Varos. And people who had been expelled from that area were already engaged in the existing units from the territory of Travnik municipality. And I here primarily refer to the 306th Brigade, the 312th Brigade, and their respective areas of responsibility. Smaller groups of people who had come from that area were already engaged in those two brigades. So people had to be taken from the already established units and attached to some other units. This was a major problem that was accompanied by moral and all other considerations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you please look at document number 1. Its number is 0468. Mr. Kulenovic, you carried a certain part of the burden during the restructuring of the army and its transformation from the Territorial Defence to operative groups. In this document under item 1, it is asked for the manoeuvre and territorial units to be organised on the extraterritorial principle. Can you please tell me, what problems did you face in your area with this regard? Was it possible to organise on the extraterritorial principle at that time?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: The military term to establish unit on the extraterritorial principle, that means to establish a unit that would be fed from a very large area. What we could do in the given circumstances, in the situation when the civilian bodies interfered with the military matters, they wanted us to form the unit on the extraterritorial principle. And they thought that ten people should be taken from one settlement, ten from another, five from a third one. This is the so-called extraterritorial establishment of units. We were not in a position to form units in such a way and we formed units primarily for these units to be attached to a certain smaller subregion. I don't know whether I've answered your question properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've told us that the role of the municipal staff had changed significantly. Can you please look at document number 5. The number of this document is 0629. Under item 3 of this document, it says that the number of staff in municipal and district staffs will be reduced to 10 per cent of the establishment. Tell me, please, how was the municipal staff organised under the circumstances and what happened to it by the end of 1993?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to orders on establishing corps brigades and lower units, the municipal staffs, including the municipal staff of Zenica, worked together with the 3rd Corps command for a certain period of time. We adapted to the situation and we exercised orders issued to us by our superior commands. What does it mean when you read here 10 per cent? If a municipal staff had a certain number of units and if the structure was what it was, then it means that only 10 per cent had to be retained and the rest were to be deployed by the corps command. In concrete terms, the municipal staff of Travnik was -- the Territorial Defence was transformed and once it lost its initial role, it kept only some 150 to 170 people in the Territorial Defence staff. In an indirect way, they were just logistical support to operational units. When I say that, they did not provide logistical support per se, they did not replenish those units, they just cooperated with the civilian bodies in order to provide for the functioning of the operational units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any units - what were their names if you had them - what was their function during that period of time, the 150 people that you mentioned or however many you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: When operational units were formed, when people were deployed to these operational units, municipal staffs - in more specific terms, my municipal staff of Travnik - retained very few people. I had only 150 people at my disposal and I was given different tasks. I'm sorry, I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What were the names of your units, what was their function?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: They had inadequate names, absolutely inadequate names, in my view. They were called anti-sabotage detachments. In the introduction to my testimony, when I introduced myself and I said who I was, I said that my specialty was reconnaissance and sabotage units because I had completed that education and a number of sabotage courses. I continued education in that field. I found it very ridiculous to see a unit where the average age of men was above 40 years of age, a unit where all the men had limited combat capabilities, or diminished combat capabilities, a unit in which men were not capable of being engaged in combat activities was a unit that was called anti-sabotage unit. This is a very simple explanation. In order for somebody to become a member of the sabotage unit, one has to learn a lot. One has to have psychological and intellectual capabilities. If somebody is to become a member of an anti-sabotage unit -- I'm not going to mention Sylvester Stallone Rambo 1 and 2, because those are just movies -- those people have to be up to 50 per cent better educated in order to be members of such anti-sabotage units. I did have those units which were called anti-sabotage units, however those units consisted of older men with diminished combat capabilities. Those were territorial units that covered the territory in the depth of the operational unit and they provided security for some less important facilities. For example, my unit provided security for the staff command of Blue Waters, the post office building, the water supply building -- actually two facilities of the water supply. And from time to time as circumstances permitted, because there were conflicts with the HVO, they also provided security for the TV relay. So we provided security for some facilities of importance for the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Since you have provided quite a lot of details with regard to the transformation of the Territorial Defence and the loss of functions of the municipal staff, can you please tell us, what were your main tasks and duties? As the commander of the municipal staff, what did you do during the first part of your term of duty up to the end of March 1993? If you can just briefly tell us that and then we will move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: What I did from the moment I was appointed towards the end of November up to the end of March was to establish units, operational brigades. I managed to do that together with the newly appointed members of the command and newly appointed members of the command of the new brigades. This was one part of my duties. The next part of my duties was the replenishment of these units. The municipal staff, which had some 7.000 men in Travnik, and these people were assigned to nine or ten regional units, these people, together with Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond their equipment, had to be redistributed to -- into those new brigades. This was a very complex task, given the circumstances. The second task that I would like to mention as being among the most difficult ones was the reception, looking after and further care for the refugees and expelled persons from Banja Luka and Prijedor. My third task was to fight civilian bodies or working with them in order to convince them that there should be a brigade, that there should also be the municipal defence staff, and that the civilian bodies had to employ their resources in order to support both the operational units because we had two in the territory as well as the municipal defence staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is quite enough. I just wanted to hear what your main tasks were. In Travnik there were some other military units. There was the Croatian Defence Council. Can you tell us, what was the relationship you had with them and what problems did you encounter as commander of the municipal staff during the first half of the year 1993?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: I would go even further back in time. When we were engaged in fighting in the town of Jajce, that is the BiH army and the HVO and as well as fighting in around Dobratic and Karaula, it was our common interest to protect this territory. Both the BiH army and the HVO had a common interest and goal, however, what I could notice at the time and subsequently what was confirmed to me through the developments, there were always dualities or dual aspects. In Travnik, there was the HVO brigade of Travnik and their primary goal was to organise the Croatian people in military and in political terms and to have them all under the HVO wing. The territory of the town of Travnik was covered by the two BiH -- HVO brigades, the one that covered the town of Travnik and the other one that -- which was the Frankopan Brigade, which covered the territory of the Bila Valley and whose territory overlapped with the responsibility of the 306th Brigade, 306th Mountain Brigade. I would like to say at this point that there were also all sorts of police units. There were -- there was a unit called The Jokers and another unit whose name I can't remember, they were also under the wing of the HVO. There were police, special police, so the HVO was a unit which was organised in military terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At any point in time were there any incidents, excesses, and what did you do to establish cooperation, or rather, did you provoke conflicts with the other military formation present in the town of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: There were incidents, there were excesses, there were a lot of them in the area of Travnik municipality. The first time I was directly involved in an excessive situation was in May 1992 when I called my manoeuvre unit from Vitez to the battlefield in Visoko. HVO units didn't allow me to pass through the territory with my vehicles. I had to provide them with a list of my men and equipment, I had to tell them the tasks I had to carry out. I had to tell them why I would be engaged in the battlefield in Visoko. This was in May 1992. Whenever I went to Visoko where I was engaged with my manoeuvre unit, or if I was taking a unit from Vitez to the Turbe battlefield, I had to pass through at least three HVO checkpoints on such occasions. So there was one at Stari Bila, Nova Bila, by the sawmill, and there was the Okuka checkpoint at a crossroads which you come across from Vitez and Travnik when you go in the direction of Novi Travnik, and it's at that checkpoint I also had to provide them with information. I was checked by another unit which should have been fighting together with me against a common enemy. While I performed my duties as the commander of the municipal staff in Travnik there were a lot of incidents. When my sector detachments were on shift, we had to provide information on the number of men involved, the number of food, the days the task would involve, we had to state how much food would be provided and for -- the kind of -- period of time this concerned. And if individuals were returning towards the Turbe battlefield, they were often maltreated, their weapons were taken away, their uniforms were taken away. There was a problem with the Borac company in Travnik - this was a textile company - because before the war this company was well-known as a producer of military uniforms. They had a huge warehouse that contained material for military uniforms. And in agreement with the civilian bodies and the management of the Borac company, these uniforms were sent to Split to be dyed there. I was aware of this and I authorised this. This was also on the basis of the authorisation provided by the regional staff as well. About 3 million metres -- well, I'm not quite sure of the number but a huge number of material was sent to Split to be dyed into camouflage colours. It was then to be returned to Travnik and uniforms were to be made for members of the BH army. This was also a significant problem. We would receive 10 to 15 per cent of the uniforms. I would receive 10 or 20 uniforms out of a hundred, the HVO would receive 70 or 80 of them. So there was material that was seized in such cases, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, as far as this issue is concerned, what sort of policies did the 3rd Corps pursue? They were your superior command, what sort of policy did they pursue as far as a possibility of a conflict breaking out with the HVO was concerned? Did the 3rd Corps issue orders telling units how they should behave in the case of incidents or in the case of an open conflict?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: As commander of the Travnik municipal staff, as a professional soldier, I often had verbal conflicts with the 3rd Corps command, and before that with the command of the Zenica regional staff, because they always ordered me to avoid large-scale conflicts at whatever cost. And they said that I should try to resolve any difficulties in a peaceful manner. And as a result, I was often placed in a very humiliating position. On two occasions I was arrested at the checkpoint at Okuka. Anto Furundzija arrested me and took me to a hotel in Vitez which is where -- well, I wouldn't say I was slapped but I was slapped by Sandic [phoen] and a commander of the operations zone, Blaskic, got me out of difficulties on a number of occasions because Blaskic and I, Blaskic and myself, worked together in Ljubljana, later on in Posnjna. I had also been his superior, so he respected me in a certain sense, so quite frequently Blaskic helped extricate me from certain difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kulenovic, could you please have a look at document number 4. It's an order from the 3rd Corps, and could you please have a look at item number 3, and tell me, is this the clearly stated position of the 3rd Corps as far as relations with the HVO are concerned at the time we have been talking about?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: I'm familiar with this document and this is one of the documents that in a certain sense made me a little angry with my superior command because attempts were made to preserve the peace, whatever the cost, although, as I have already said, I was frequently in very humiliating situations. But it's true to say that what is stated here is not just theoretical. This was the situation in practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at document number 21, DH056 -- 0656. Are you familiar with this document and could you comment on it?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: I'm familiar with this document. I can recognise my signature and the signature of the commander of the Travnik Brigade, Colonel Filip Filipovic. To provide you with additional details in relation to the previous order that we have been referring to, I think there were a number of orders stating that incidents or conflictual situations should be resolved peacefully. I went to see Mr. Filipovic, Colonel Filipovic, on a number of occasions and since I knew Blaskic, I frequently saw him, too, and I tried to resolve all the difficulties, any conflictual situations, through agreement. I tried to calm tensions that might lead to something much worse. I think this is one of the public statements that were issued. It says the 1st Corps, the command of the 7th Brigade. I don't know whose stamp this is but this is my signature. It was drafted by myself and by Filip and we always tried to avoid such conflictual situations. This is one of the statements that we used, that we issued through the media, through the radio, through the newspapers in order to inform the people that any problems would be jointly dealt with, that I as Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond commander of the Territorial Defence staff and Colonel Filipovic would try to resolve together.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In line 22 it mentions the 7th Brigade. You in fact mentioned the stamp at the top where we can see the stamp of this brigade that also received this document. Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I wasn't quite clear about the stamp at the top, but it's clear to me now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kulenovic, you said that this was a public statement and that it contains certain conclusions. As a soldier you probably also issued orders to your units in relation to this subject. Can you tell me whether the army implemented these conclusions referred to here; and what was the HVO's attitude with regard to these conclusions?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: As a commander of the Travnik municipal staff, I could not directly relay these conclusions to operation units. But I issued direct orders to my units, to the anti-sabotage unit. I had also informed brigade commanders of such conclusions, the commander of the 312th Brigade and the commander of the 306th Brigade. I also provided such information to commanders who were in the Travnik -- who were in Travnik or in the field. At this time I was still the commander of the municipal defence staff. These conclusions were really implemented by the municipal staff, and I can also say that the units in the territory of Travnik, in the territory of the municipality of Travnik, also respected and implemented these conclusions. I in a certain sense was the person who dealt with such matters in Travnik, and I established contact with officials in the operative zone of Central Bosnia and officials in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me whether the attempts that you made yielded results. Thanks to these efforts, was a conflict in Travnik avoided or did events unfold in some different way?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, these agreements of ours and these conclusions and the statements that we made through the media only helped us to find temporary solutions to certain problems. Because as time passed by, the problems became more substantial as far as the relation between the BH army and the HVO is concerned. This also concerned the municipal authorities. They also had a lot of conflicts, there was also a lot of antagonism there. So all these conclusions had a temporary nature and we were putting out a fire that was smoldering.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kulenovic, have a look at document number 22, DH823, and could you please tell me whether you recognise this document. Does this document reflect the situation in Travnik at the beginning of April 1993?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: I can recognise this document. I am very familiar with it. I drafted a significant part of this document, but the person responsible for the document was my assistant for security, Smajic, Mesud. At the time we didn't have ranks. I am familiar with this document and with all the events referred to here. I am also familiar with events that aren't referred to here or not in detail. But, for example, it says that 2200 hours shooting could be heard. You don't have a full description of the event here, but I know that a grenade was thrown at my MP unit which was securing a hospital at the time. For no reason at all, two grenades were thrown from the fourth floor and a burst of fire was opened from an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After these events, where did the HVO units deploy and what sort of position was Travnik in after the event and what sort of position were the army units in Travnik in?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: While I was in Travnik or while I was the commander of the Travnik municipal staff, I never noticed a big HVO unit. They were always somewhere around, but they kept moving around, they kept redeploying. I never saw a large unit. I was never in a position to say, here we have a large and organised unit. But as far as my units are concerned, the municipal defence staff units are concerned and the operative units of the army, well, we were in a position to form companies and a battalion after a certain period of time, and it was possible to notice the presence of an organised military unit then. But what is important to note is that the smaller units that were deployed throughout the town of Travnik from the hospital, the nursery, the school, the warning centre, et cetera, that's where we had a smaller unit, a platoon perhaps, then there was the hotel, the Sedisic [phoen] feature, et cetera, et cetera, but these units were deployed outside the town of Travnik. On the whole they were deployed in the immediate vicinity of Travnik. They were deployed in -- on elevations from which it was possible to control or to observe everything that was happening in the town of Travnik. These features are the features of Vilenica. There was a relay station there that I secured with a unit. But we were then redeployed in a military manner, in a rough manner. Then there was Hajdareve Njive above the hospital for pulmonary diseases. This is now the Travnik cantonal hospital. So I've mentioned Hajdareve Njive, and then there was Velika and Mala Beca [phoen], just above Plava Voda, Blue Water, the entrance to Travnik. So they had surrounded the town and they had the fire power to control it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have a look at document number 10, 0958, and could you tell me what this document is about, what were your duties within that organ, and what sort of tasks did that organ have? Do you recognise the document?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can recognise the document. I know this document. After the events in Central Bosnia, in Vitez above all, after the massacre in Ahmici and in order to prevent further escalations and opening on the third front, after these events the 3rd Corps command ordered me as one of the officers in the zone of responsibility of Travnik to become member of the joint command of the BH army and the HVO. I was to be an operations officer in that joint command. I know all these people who are mentioned here, they know me, too, and we knew each other from before. Initially the command's task was to deal with problems that were a result of the conflict in the Lasva area. They were to deal with these problems to an extent this was possible. And then later on the command was to carry out and plan joint combat operations against our common enemy. First of all we had to deal with the problems that were a result of the conflict in the Lasva area and then we were to plan and carry out joint operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How did you, representatives of the BiH army, approach this task of organising joint combat activities? Did the work in that command yield any results? If not, tell us why.

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: If you'll allow me, I would like to provide you with a very short analysis and tell you something about the people who were appointed to the joint command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You don't have to do that because we've had other witnesses who testified about that and there will be some others in the future. Let's be rational with the time. Can you please tell us whether you were engaged on any of the tasks, how you worked, and did the command achieve anything.

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: I told you what our primary task was, and since I knew the territory and people in the municipality of Travnik, I absolutely worked towards dealing with all the problems in the town. And the four of us who are mentioned here on the part of the BiH army, we absolutely took our task very seriously when it came to the planning and engagement in joint combat. I'm sure that we were able to provide a complete overview of the units in the region of Travnik. We had an overview of the number of arms and combat capabilities of such units; we provided an overview of communications systems; we did everything and we put everything on the table to enable all of us to talk. At the same time, members of the HVO, those who were appointed to the joint command, they would always tell us that their units had not been established, due to the conflicts they were being restructured, the units didn't exist, and so on and so forth. On the one hand we on our part did everything we could and we approached the task very seriously. At the same time, the HVO did nothing, they were not serious. At first they did come to work regularly; however, after some five, six, or ten days they started avoiding their duties, they start -- they failed to appear in the facility where we met, which was the cellar of the post office building in Travnik. Every time they came, they insisted on arriving in the armoured personnel carrier provided to them by UNPROFOR. So we worked very well and HVO, to my mind, did not take their duties seriously and they didn't work. And this command failed in their duties when it came to preparation for joint combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kulenovic, during that period of time did you assume any other duty? Were you appointed to another duty? If that was the case, can you tell us, what duties did you assume?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: At one point in time I had three duties: I was a commander of the municipal defence staff of Travnik, I was a member of the joint command with the members of the HVO, and at the same time since the command failed to perform its duties and I did not have that many duties after a certain time, General Alagic proposed that I should become the operations officer in the Bosanska Krajina OG. There I prepared and monitored combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kulenovic, let me move on to a completely different topic. You were the commander of the municipal defence staff in Travnik. In your capacity, did you become acquainted with the existence of some foreigners from African and Asian countries who had arrived in the territory of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew that there were such individuals in Travnik. In my view, they were humanitarian workers and they were engaged in humanitarian activities. They brought food, I don't know where from and how. In any case, I was interested in that because I had spoken with Klotz [phoen], the logistical centre of Travnik, and it is through them that these people arranged their business. I saw them but they were never armed, they were never under my command, they were never under the command of any of the operational units of the 306th, 312th, or 317th Brigades. The command building was near Blue Waters, Plava Voda, it was very close to the multi-coloured mosque; that's where I saw them. They came to that mosque to perform their religious services. That's where I saw them most often.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said you moved to the operational service of the Krajina OG. Did the data from subordinate units come to you? What data did you receive in the operational centre when it came to your resubordinated units or your subordinated units?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: What I did as an operations officer in the OG was to receive information on the number of men, the quantity of equipment, the combat activities underway, combat activities under preparation, reactions to our combat operations on the part of the enemy. So all this data arrived in the operations centre of the Bosanska Krajina OG, and the information came from all the units that was -- that were in the area covered by the Bosanska Krajina OG. In cooperation with the commander and on the orders of the commander and his deputy, I would often inspect these units. That's how I knew what the number of men in those units was, what equipment they had at their disposal, and I also knew about the developments that were taking place in the unit on its left flank, on its right flank, and in the depth of its defence. So in very general terms I was abreast of the situation in the area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to my question you've told us that in your capacity as a commander of a municipal defence staff you had nothing to do with these foreigners and they had nothing to do with you. When you arrived in the operations centre of the Bosanska Krajina OG in June, on the strength of the units that were subordinated to the Bosanska Krajina OG, did you see or did you receive any information to the effect that these Arabs, Mujahedins, or these foreigners from African and Asian countries were on the strength of your units or in other words on the strength of the operation group?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: I said that I was familiar with the number of men and equipment, with the combat operations in -- that certain units were engaged in. I didn't have any information, none of the units ever told me or wrote to me in any of their combat reports that they had Arabs or any other men that did not belong to the establishment structure of these units. And I repeat, I had a good overview of the troops and the equipment and everything that was important for the functioning of those units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, maybe this is a good time for a break. I will need another ten minutes to complete with the examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We are going to make a 25-minute break. We shall resume at 5 to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll now resume and I give the floor to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kulenovic, before the break you were saying that as an operations officer and operations and training organ you would visit your units to see the state of combat readiness they were in and to perform all your other duties. Tell me, while performing these duties with members of the 3rd Corps command, did you at any point in time come across the problem of the Mujahedin, or rather, did some of your subordinate units inform you of the existence of such a problem?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'll provide you with an example. Naturally when visiting the units and positions with the operations and training organ I visited the zone of responsibility of the 306th Brigade on the -- on the Vlasic plateau and examined the situation in the zone of responsibility of that unit. And through speaking to the troops I discovered that there were certain problems in the unit because of the presence of these foreigners - I don't know how to call them - but they had an influence on the combat readiness of the unit. They were trying to go after men, recruit men from their units by providing them with presents, money, food, et cetera, and troops complained about this on the Vlasic plateau. They said that they had such problems because these foreigners were trying to persuade them to leave the units and join them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kulenovic, were these foreigners, these Mujahedin subordinated to the 306th or some other army unit that was part of the Bosanska Krajina OG, or rather of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll repeat what I was saying a minute ago. As an operations officer in the operations group, I had information on the unit, the men in the unit, and the equipment they had. And when reviewing this information I never came across information according to which there were men in one of those units who weren't actually part of that unit. To be more specific, there were no foreigners in the 306th Brigade. I'm sure there were no foreigners in the 312th, in the 17th, and in other units that were part of the operations group. There were no foreigners; this could be seen when one had a look at the lists and this could be seen in fact in the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kulenovic, did you at any point in time come across information according to which the El Mujahid detachment had been formed in 1993?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did find out that such a detachment had been formed, but I was never involved in its establishment nor did I know where this took place and I didn't know the sort of task that the detachment would be involved in. I was not a participant in establishing the chain of command and establishing the other elements that are necessary for the formation of such a unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kulenovic, tell me whether you had access to an order issued by the 3rd Corps according to which that detachment should be resubordinated to the Bosanska Krajina OG for combat operations, and did the commander make any attempts to place these men under his command? Do you have any information on this matter?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as an officer in the operations group, I had to know which units were to become part of the constant structure or the temporary structure. I know that the El Mujahid unit - again I don't know when and where it was formed or on what basis - but I know at one point in time it was supposed to be resubordinated, but the word "resubordinated" or "subordinated" or "attached," these terms could be discussed, but I do know that this unit or part of this unit participated one of our brigades in combat operation and because of the way they engaged in combat I know that one of our units sustained significant losses. So after one hour of fighting our 17th Krajina Brigade had 12 dead, about 80 or 90 wounded men, et cetera. So in a fairly short period of time, they sustained losses that were far too great.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Kulenovic, could you tell me whether to the best of your knowledge these foreigners, the Mujahedin from the El Mujahid detachment at any time in 1993 in fact placed themselves under the command and control of the operations group or its subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know the Mujahedin or the El Mujahid detachment were never placed under the command of the Bosanska Krajina OG, at least not on the basis of the documents available, nor did they ever become part of the structure of the Bosanska Krajina OG. And a minute ago I said they did participate with us in combat operations, they participated in combat operations with our unit, and because of the way they engaged in combat, we sustained very significant losses.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kulenovic, you and the Bosanska Krajina OG, did you have the possibility of going to that detachment and carrying out investigations, checkups, et cetera? Was this possible to the command and the members of the Bosanska Krajina OG staff in 1993?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: General Alagic on one occasion, and this was at the beginning of August, I think, took me there. We tried to enter the camp that they had in the village of -- well, it was a village above Mehurici in the immediate vicinity of the Mehurici settlement. We wanted to persuade them to join or become part of the system of command and control. We wanted to prepare them to carry out certain combat operations, but at the entrance to the camp we were received in a very rough manner, no respect was shown, especially not for General Alagic, the commander of the OG, nor did they show respect for me. We were taken to some building, asked what we wanted. As I had a cigarette, I was an infidel. So this was their attitude towards General Alagic and myself. And as far as I know, we didn't manage to persuade them or to reach an agreement with them on joint action or an agreement or engaging them within the OG. I don't know how this unit was subsequently engaged.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you have just mentioned August now, could you just say whether this was after the El Mujahid detachment had been formed. Was it after the formation that you went to talk to them with General Alagic about their subordination?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: As I said, I didn't know exactly when the El Mujahid detachment was formed, but when we went there all I knew was we were going to the El Mujahid detachment to see whether we could engage them in the upcoming combat operations. As to the order on the basis of which this was done, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You have just said -- you have just told us about what happened with Commander Alagic. Were there any other bodies of yours, any other organs of yours, that could control that detachment up until the end of 1993?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, in the training camp - I'm not sure what it was called, but in the camp where they resided - no one from the BH army was able to enter that camp. I'm referring to members of the OG but also to members of the units that were there, the 306th, the 312th, part of the 7th Muslim, there was a battalion in Travnik then, there was the 27th that was being formed at that time, and there was some other attached units or units that were moving through our zone. But none of these units, no members from these units were able to enter the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kulenovic. You have just said at one point you had to perform various duties and the role of the municipal staff gradually changed, it was being disbanded and you became part of the OG. Have a look at the document 1501, document 17, please. This is a proposal from the 3rd Corps to the supreme command staff. Under number 6, under item 6, there is a proposal that concerns the Travnik municipal staff. Tell me, do you know whether Travnik municipal staff continued to exist, or after this proposal was it disbanded?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: After this proposal was made, the Travnik municipal staff was disbanded as a military structure on the basis of this order and the proposals that were subsequently made. But on the basis of these suggestions, elements from the municipal staff became part of these units, as stated in this proposal and later on in an order. On the basis of that order, I was assigned to the OG, and I no longer performed any duties in the municipal staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kulenovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this concludes my examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll now turn to the other defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll now give the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. My name is Daryl Mundis and along with my colleagues here today we represent the Prosecution in this case. I have just a few questions for you, sir. Before I ask those I would simply like to inform you that it's not my intention in any way to confuse you, so if there's any question that I ask you that you don't understand, simply say so and I'll rephrase the question so that we're absolutely clear with respect to what I'm asking you. Let me start by talking a little bit about or asking you a few questions about when you first came to the Travnik municipal staff. I believe you said that was the end of August or the beginning of September 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The end of August was the time when the procedure started. I don't remember the exact date when I joined. I believe that it was at the beginning of September, either on the 2nd or the 3rd. So we are talking about a five-day period when this all happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, at the time you joined that staff, can you tell us, please, the precise title of that unit that you were part of in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived in Travnik there were still units being organised to put up resistance against the enemy. The municipal defence staff existed and it was subordinated to the regional staff in Zenica and further up the hierarchy to the supreme staff in Sarajevo. So municipal staffs were subordinated to the regional staffs, and the regional staffs were subordinated to the state staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, when you first arrived at the Travnik municipal staff at the beginning of September 1992, who was your immediate superior in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived in Travnik and when I reported to the duty, I was appointed the assistant commander of the municipal defence staff, and my superior was Ribo Haso. At that time ranks did not exist, we just had commanders, their assistants, their deputies. So my commander was Ribo Haso.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how long after your arrival did Ribo Haso remain as the commander of that staff in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: I assumed my duties during the first couple days of September and Ribo Haso was my superior up to the second half of November. I'm not sure about the date. It could have been either the 18th or the 20th of November. And then due to the commander's illness, I was appointed the commander first by an oral order which was followed by a written order confirming that. That happened around that time and I can't give you the exact date again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's fine, sir. I just wanted to be clear that the fact is that when you first arrived in Travnik at the beginning of September 1992, Ribo Haso was the commander and then some point in mid-November, due to his illness, he left and you in fact became the commander of the municipal staff in Travnik. Is that an accurate summary?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber a little bit about any type of military or combat activities that occurred within the town of Travnik from the time you arrived in early September until the time you assumed command of the municipal staff in mid-November 1992.

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: In the town of Travnik itself, in its settled part, there were no combat activities, at least not such that I would consider combat activities as a professional soldier. Combat activities were taking place in Bijelo Bucje, Vrbe [phoen], Turbe and the plateau of Vlasic in Gornje Meokrnje. These were more or less the lines that the army and the HVO used to defend the territory against the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor. We performed combat activities there. Those were defence activities because the Serbians and Montenegrins launched attacks against us. In most of the operations, we defended ourselves. Parts of the units from Jajce, after Jajce fell, withdrew towards us, they joined us, we received those units. And also when the part of the municipality of Travnik fell, the local detachment from Karaula joined us as well. Those were the major combat operations. And on the defence line on the Vlasic plateau, we defended the plateau against Serbs and Montenegrins with whatever means we had at our disposal. Those were the major combat operations that were taking place when I was a member of the municipal defence staff of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, let me again focus your attention on the period from the beginning of September 1992 through the time that you became the commander of the municipal staff in the middle of November 1992. So I'm asking you about that two-and-a-half-month period when you first arrived at the municipal staff in Travnik. During that period of time, did you remain physically present, you personally, in the town of Travnik during that two-and-a-half-month period, or were you travelling out or visiting other units in the areas outlying Travnik, the town of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: A little while ago I mentioned defence and defence activities that the municipal defence staff of Travnik was engaged in. I also mentioned the facilities and the centres where I stayed, where I was engaged, and pursuant to the orders of Ribo Haso, this is where I also commanded some activities. I'm a professional soldier, and at that time, there were no military experts who could organise defence in a professional manner. I had to stay in Bijelo Bucje, in Karaula, in the village of Dobratici, and in that general region. I inspected 90 per cent of the lines on the Vlasic plateau myself. This means I was not always in the town of Travnik in the staff building. As an operative, I had to be present on the defence lines wherever combats were taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So it's fair then to say, sir, that during this two-and-a-half-month period you travelled to a number of locations in the immediate vicinity of Travnik town in order to inspect the troops at these front line positions. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During this same time period, sir, what if anything was the commander Haso Ribo doing? Was he similarly making any inspections? What -- to the best of your knowledge, what was the commander doing during that time period, September to mid-November, 1992?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: In military jargon speaking, I was not duty-bound to know what he was doing. I was duty-bound to carry out things on his orders. In any case, Ribo Haso did go to the positions or send the five of us who were familiar with the ground, who were familiar with the men, who were familiar with the deployment of equipment, and he also had a lot of locals who were either reserve officers of the former JNA or were the JNA officers who had returned. So he trusted us and he trusted our opinion. And based on our opinion, he was able to draw conclusions at our briefings and meetings. So we worked as a team, as real staff, and I repeat, Ribo Haso, he himself inspected a lot of the lines, either on his own or with us or he would put together teams that would inspect various units, artillery units, infantry units. It all depended on what was to be inspected, that's how he decided what kind of teams to form to send out to inspect the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So I take it then, sir, from what you've just told us, that Haso Ribo did not remain in the municipal staff headquarters every single day throughout that time period, September through mid-November 1992. He in fact was out examining positions and units on the front lines.

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. However, we had an agreement that all of us who were of the same generation, we often organised teams like I've just told you. A team would be, for example, put together in order to inspect the infantry unit. I would be the head of that team.
